drafts.title: 36 to 45 cents. My report card for 13 charging stops (pack AP2, chargers, human moment)
drafts.window: Tue 11 AM-12 PM MT (very strong cell). Don't run it the same hour as #1.
drafts.angle: Still his best unposted trip story: an awards list wives and older travelers want before their first EV road trip. New hook today: Ionna just passed 200 sites, so tagging @ionnaofficial with 'best bathroom of 13 stops' gives a brand a reason to repost. If he's already rolling home, frame it as 'grading them again on the way back.' Graded roundup only; no trip total, no national averages (both LIVE).
bullets: His stops ranged 36c a kWh (Rifle and Frisco Superchargers) to 45c (Little General, Columbia MO).
Best bathroom: Ionna Limon. @ionnaofficial already replied to his post: "Thanks for juicin' up with us!"
Best surprise: Kuttawa KY V3 Superchargers had WiFi; he pulled the 14.3.12 update while charging.
Ionna passed 200 sites (about 1,666 stalls in 30 states, many at Circle K and Wawa), per EVI weekly news; only about 10% of new Q3 fast-charger sites were rural.
J.D. Power 2026 EVX study (Aug 12): owners are happiest charging at gas stations, convenience stores and restaurants, least happy at dealerships. His best stops match.
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
36 to 45 cents a kWh across 13 stops.

Best bathroom: Ionna Limon.
Best store: Little General.
Best surprise: WiFi in Kuttawa.
Worst stop: [___].

[photo: collage of stops]

What's the best charging stop you've ever found?

LONGER VERSION:
Thirteen charging stops from Grand Junction to Kentucky. Here's my report card.

Cheapest: Rifle and Frisco Superchargers, 36 cents a kWh.
Priciest: Little General in Columbia, Missouri, 45 cents. Worth it. Nicest store of the trip.
Best bathroom: Ionna in Limon. Clean, bright, coffee that wasn't sad. @ionnaofficial
Best surprise: Kuttawa, Kentucky. WiFi at the Superchargers, and my car updated itself while we ate.
Worst stop: [___, and why.]

Funny thing. The best stops weren't about the charger. They were about the store and the bathroom. A big J.D. Power survey of EV owners found the same thing.

Out in the country the good stops are still spread thin. [One line on the longest gap between good stops.]

[One line from my wife: her favorite stop and why.]

Round two on the way home. What's the best charging stop you've ever found?

drafts.title: 20 cents a month. Louisiana votes Thursday on making power customers pay to study small reactors (pack AP8, SMR, who pays)
drafts.window: Tue 9-10 PM MT or Wed 1-3 PM MT (must go before Thursday's vote). Skip Wed 1-3 PM if #3 lands there.
drafts.angle: A tiny, concrete bill number with a vote this week. Keep it strictly to who pays, no politics, no reactor specs. Only SMR item this week; never posted.
bullets: Louisiana Public Service Commission vote scheduled Thursday, Oct 22, on the Louisiana Advanced Nuclear Exploration program (The Center Square via American Press, Oct 16).

As proposed: 20 cents a month on customer bills, about $4 million a year across the three big investor-owned utilities, for small modular reactor and microreactor feasibility studies and early licensing prep.
Commissioner Eric Skrmetta's proposed amendment: utilities spend up to $2 million and ask to recover it in rates later.
Commissioner Davante Lewis supports more nuclear but says it "should not happen on the backs of ratepayers."
20 cents a month is $2.40 a year per customer.
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
20 cents a month. That's what Louisiana regulators may add to power bills to study small nuclear reactors.

Vote is Thursday.

Would you pay 20 cents a month for that, or should the power companies foot the bill?

LONGER VERSION:
20 cents a month. $2.40 a year. That's what Louisiana regulators may add to everybody's power bill to study small nuclear reactors.

The vote is Thursday. The money, about $4 million a year, would pay for studies and early licensing work at the three big utilities.

One commissioner wants the utilities to front the money instead and ask to get paid back later. Another says he likes nuclear but it shouldn't come out of customers' pockets.

Here's my take: [___. Would I pay $2.40 a year for a shot at steadier, cheaper power down the road? Or should the companies that profit carry the risk?]

I'm not in Louisiana, but this is coming to a lot of states. Would you pay 20 cents a month for it?
